title: Prototype and Pressure-Test the Plan (Lab)
summary: Students prototype their approved plan on the board, break it on purpose with a tricky curated input, and design an if-then fallback branch that keeps a person in the loop.
objectives: Prototype the prompt structure and pressure-test the plan against a tricky input.
Add a fallback branch for when the output fails a check.
Record what changed and why after the pressure test.

body: A plan on paper looks tidy. Today you find out how it behaves under pressure. You will build a quick prototype, then throw your hardest inputs at it on purpose - the missing item, the messy note, the two-in-one line. When it stumbles, you will not hide the failure; you will design a fallback branch that catches it safely. Engineers stress-test bridges before people cross them. You will stress-test your solution before it is trusted.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can run my prompt structure on a normal input and read the output.
I can pressure-test it with a tricky input and spot where it fails.
I can add a fallback branch that says what to do when a check fails.
I can record the change I made and the reason for it.

terms.definition: A first working version built quickly to see how a design really behaves.
Deliberately trying a tricky input to reveal a weak spot.
An unusual input at the edge of what a solution expects, like a missing or double value.
A planned 'if a check fails, then...' response that handles a failure safely.
A label for what went wrong: wrong, unclear, or missing.

sections.heading: Prototype first, judge second
body: A [[prototype]] is a fast first version. Running it shows how your design behaves, not just how you hoped it would.
The teacher runs your prompt on the board with a normal curated input. You read the output and decide: did it meet the goal?

sections.heading: Design the fallback branch
body: When a check fails, a good solution follows a [[fallback branch]] instead of giving a confident wrong answer.
Write it as 'If the check fails, then ___ and ask a person.' Keeping a human in the loop is part of responsible design.
Remember: only curated, made-up inputs - never real names or personal data.

sections.label: Hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: You will prototype your approved plan, pressure-test it, and add a fallback branch. The teacher runs the AI on the board; you do not log in. Log every run.
items: Copy your prompt structure into the prototype slot of your log.
Watch the normal-input run on the board and record whether it met the goal.
Pressure-test with a tricky curated input and record the error type.
Write your fallback branch as an if-then sentence that asks a person.
Log the one change you made and the reason it will help.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which tricky input broke the most prototypes, and why?
Why is a handled failure safer than a confident wrong answer?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the weak spot your pressure test exposed.
Write how your fallback branch will handle it next week.

worksheet.title: Week 7 - Lab - Worksheet | Prototype and Pressure-Test the Plan (Lab)

questions.prompt: Bilal's prototype has the task "label each found item as clothing, devices or other". For his pressure test he uses the tricky note "found: a charger and a scarf". The output reads: "devices". Using the lesson's three error-type labels, which error type should he log?

options.text: Missing - the note held two items and one of them has come back with no label.
Wrong - the charger has been put into the incorrect category.
Unclear - the word "devices" could mean more than one thing.
No error - the prompt asked for a label, and one label came back.

feedback.correct: Right - the charger is labelled correctly, so nothing is wrong; what the two-in-one note exposed is a whole item being dropped.
feedback.incorrect: The label "devices" fits the charger, so this is not a wrong answer - the weak spot is the scarf, which never got a label at all.

questions.prompt: Bilal now writes up that failure in his build/test log. Choose the TWO entries that meet what the lesson asks for: a fallback branch and a logged reason.

options.text: Fallback: "If a note names more than one item, then label each item on its own line, and if one still does not fit, label it other and ask a person."
Reason: "My pressure test showed a two-in-one note loses an item, so splitting the note before labelling stops items being dropped."
Fallback: "If the output looks wrong, then run the prompt again until it looks right."
Fallback: "If a note names more than one item, then label the first item and move on."
Reason: "I changed my prompt because I wanted the output to sound better."

feedback.correct: Yes - the branch is an if-then that handles the failure he actually saw and keeps a person in the loop, and the reason points back to what the run showed.
feedback.incorrect: Re-running until it looks right, or labelling only the first item, still loses the scarf, and "I wanted it to sound better" is not a reason drawn from the test.

questions.prompt: Maya says: "A prototype that always gives a confident answer, even on a messy input, is safer than one that stops and asks a person." Is Maya right?

feedback.correct: Correct - a confident wrong answer gets used without anyone noticing, while a handled failure sends the messy case to a person who can sort it out.
feedback.incorrect: Think about who catches the mistake: a confident answer on a messy input hides the failure, but a fallback branch that asks a person makes it visible and safe.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the lab routine into the order the lesson gives them.

items.text: Copy the approved prompt structure into the prototype slot of the log.
Watch the normal-input run on the board and record whether it met the goal.
Pressure-test with a tricky curated input and record the error type.
Write the fallback branch as an if-then sentence that asks a person.
Log the one change made and the reason it will help.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the normal run comes before the pressure test so you know the prototype works at all, and the branch is written only once a real weak spot has shown itself.
feedback.incorrect: You cannot design a fallback for a failure you have not seen yet: prototype, run it normally, pressure-test it, then write the branch and log the reason.

questions.prompt: Four groups pressure-tested the same found-items prototype and each exposed a different weak spot. Match each weak spot to the fallback branch that handles it.

left.text: The note held two items, but only one came back with a label.
The output said "maybe clothing, or possibly other".
The note had no item written on it, and the output named an item anyway.

right.text: If a note names more than one item, then label each item separately and ask a person about any item left over.
If the label does not match the item's own words, then flag that row for a person to re-check before it is posted.
If the answer offers more than one label, then leave the row unlabelled and ask a person to decide.
If the input has no item to label, then reply "no item found" and ask a person, instead of guessing.

feedback.correct: Well matched - a fallback branch is only useful when it answers the exact failure the pressure test exposed.
feedback.incorrect: Match each branch to what actually went wrong: a dropped item, a mislabelled item, an undecided label, and an invented item each need a different if-then.

formative.targets: Checks that the plan survives a tricky input and gains a fallback branch
formative.check: Build/test log review: one normal run, one pressure test, one fallback branch, one logged change
formative.successCriteria: Prototype is run, a tricky input exposes a weak spot, and a fallback branch plus a logged reason are added.
formative.evidence: Completed build/test log with fallback branch.
